title: Isaiah
lead: Isaiah son of Amoz, a prophet in Jerusalem from about 740 to 700 BC, under kings Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz and Hezekiah, and the book that carries his name. Many scholars hold that chapters 40–66 come from later prophets in his tradition, during and after the exile.

sections.b: Isaiah, in Hebrew Yesha'yahu, 'the LORD saves', was a prophet in Jerusalem from about 740 BC, the year King Uzziah died (Isaiah 6:1), until at least 701 BC, when Sennacherib of Assyria besieged the city (Isaiah 36–37). He spoke to kings face to face: to Ahaz at the conduit of the upper pool (Isaiah 7:3) and to Hezekiah in the crisis of 701 and in his illness (2 Kings 19–20; Isaiah 37–38). He was married to 'the prophetess' and gave his sons names that were messages: Shear-jashub, 'a remnant will turn back', and Maher-shalal-hash-baz, 'quick to the plunder' (Isaiah 7:3; Isaiah 8:1–4, 18). Chronicles says he wrote the history of Uzziah and of Hezekiah (2 Chronicles 26:22; 2 Chronicles 32:32). Once he walked barefoot and stripped for three years as a sign against Egypt (Isaiah 20). The Bible does not tell how he died; later tradition says Manasseh had him sawn in two.

sections.h: The book that carries his name
sections.b: The book of Isaiah has 66 chapters. Chapters 1–39 are mostly set in Isaiah's own lifetime and speak of Assyria; chapters 40–66 speak to exiles in Babylon and to the community that returned, and name Cyrus of Persia (Isaiah 44:28; Isaiah 45:1). Jewish and Christian tradition, and many conservative scholars today, hold that Isaiah wrote the whole book, foreseeing the exile and return. Most critical scholars since Döderlein (1775) and Duhm (1892) assign chapters 40–55 to an anonymous prophet of the exile ('Second Isaiah') and 56–66 to prophets after the return ('Third Isaiah'), with later material in 1–39 as well. Recent scholarship stresses that, whoever wrote it, the book was edited to be read as one, held together by themes such as 'the Holy One of Israel', Zion, the remnant and the highway home. The book's page sets out each view in full.

sections.b: The New Testament names Isaiah about twenty times, more than any other prophet, and quotes or echoes the book far more often. John the Baptist is 'the voice' of Isaiah 40:3 (Mark 1:2–3; John 1:23). Jesus reads Isaiah 61:1–2 in the synagogue at Nazareth (Luke 4:16–21), and explains his parables with Isaiah 6:9–10 (Matthew 13:14–15). Matthew finds Immanuel (Isaiah 7:14; Matthew 1:23), the light in Galilee (Isaiah 9:1–2; Matthew 4:14–16) and the servant (Isaiah 42:1–4; Matthew 12:17–21). Philip begins from Isaiah 53 to tell an Ethiopian official about Jesus (Acts 8:30–35). John says Isaiah 'saw his glory' (John 12:41). Paul draws on Isaiah again and again in Romans 9–11. Many of these quotations follow the Greek translation rather than the Hebrew.

sections.h: Isaiah in Jewish and Christian tradition
sections.b: Sirach, about 180 BC, praises Isaiah as the great prophet who 'comforted those who mourned in Zion' (Sirach 48:22–25). The Great Isaiah Scroll from Qumran, copied about 125 BC, is the oldest complete book of the Bible, and more copies of Isaiah were found at Qumran than of any other prophet. In the synagogue Isaiah gives the seven haftarot of consolation read after the Ninth of Av, and the seraphim's 'Holy, holy, holy' (Isaiah 6:3) is said in every Kedushah. The Talmud and the Martyrdom and Ascension of Isaiah tell that King Manasseh had him sawn in two (Babylonian Talmud, Yevamot 49b), a story many think Hebrews 11:37 alludes to. Jerome called Isaiah 'an evangelist rather than a prophet', and the church has called his book 'the fifth gospel'; it fills the readings of Advent, Christmas and Good Friday, and much of Handel's Messiah.
